title: Hananiah Breaks the Yoke
summary: In the temple, the prophet Hananiah announces in the LORD's name that within two years God will break Babylon's yoke and bring back the exiles, King Jeconiah, and the temple vessels. Jeremiah answers that he wishes it were so, but that prophets of peace must be proved by events; Hananiah then breaks the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck. Later the LORD sends Jeremiah back to say that the wooden yoke will be replaced by one of iron and that Hananiah will die within the year, and two months later he does.
story: Chapter 27 ended with Jeremiah wearing a yoke and warning against prophets who promised that the temple vessels would soon return from Babylon. Now one of those prophets steps forward by name, in the same temple and in the same year. This is the book's clearest head-to-head contest between a true and a false prophet, and it dramatizes the questions raised in 23:9-40 about how to tell them apart. Hananiah's promise of two years stands against Jeremiah's seventy (25:11), and the letter of chapter 29 will warn the exiles not to believe men like him.
historical:
The date is the fifth month of Zedekiah's fourth year, around the summer of 594 or 593 BC, a few years after the first deportation of 597 BC and in the same period as the envoys' meeting of chapter 27. Hananiah promises the return of Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), who was still alive in Babylon and whom many in Judah regarded as the rightful king even while his uncle Zedekiah reigned. Cuneiform tablets found in Babylon, listing oil rations issued to foreign captives, name Jehoiachin as king of Judah along with his sons, confirming that he was kept at the Babylonian court in these years. He would in fact be released from prison, but not until about 561 BC, some thirty-seven years after his exile (52:31-34), and he never returned home.

Hananiah came from Gibeon, a town a few miles northwest of Jerusalem that had been assigned to the priests (Joshua 21:17). Nothing else is known of him.
cultural:
Prophets in Judah were public figures who spoke in the temple courts before priests and people, and a prophetic sign-act was understood to carry the weight of the word it enacted. When Hananiah broke Jeremiah's yoke, the crowd would have taken it as more than theater; he was claiming that the thing signified was being broken too. His language exactly mirrors Jeremiah's, with the same formula, “This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says,” so the people had no outward way of telling who was right.

Israel's law gave two tests. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 says that a prophet whose word does not come to pass has not spoken from the LORD. Deuteronomy 13:1-5 says that even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he leads people away from the LORD, and that such a prophet is to die because he has taught rebellion against God. Jeremiah's words in verse 16, that Hananiah has preached rebellion against the LORD, echo that law directly.
literary: The story is built in two scenes separated by an interval. In the first (verses 1 to 11) Hananiah speaks and acts, Jeremiah responds with restraint, and then Jeremiah simply walks away. In the second (verses 12 to 17) the LORD speaks to Jeremiah, who returns with a word of judgment, and the narrator closes with a flat report of its fulfillment. Both men are called “the prophet” throughout, a deliberate even-handedness that lets the events, not the labels, decide between them. The wordplay turns on the yoke: Hananiah breaks a yoke of wood, and God answers with a yoke of iron. The dating is precise, fifth month to seventh month, so that the reader can see Jeremiah's word fulfilled within the year while Hananiah's two years never arrive.

outline.t: Hananiah's prophecy: the yoke broken within two years
Jeremiah's reply: Amen, but let the word be proved
Hananiah breaks the yoke; Jeremiah goes his way
A yoke of iron in place of the yoke of wood

doctrines.note: Hananiah sounds exactly like a true prophet. The chapter shows that the form of words proves nothing; what matters is whether God has sent the messenger, which is shown by agreement with God's covenant word and, in time, by fulfillment (verse 9).
Rejecting God's discipline makes it harder, not lighter: the wooden yoke becomes iron. Hananiah's death shows that speaking falsely in God's name is a grave matter, not a harmless mistake.
Jeremiah's “Amen” in verse 6 is sincere. He does not want disaster, and he would gladly be proved wrong. True prophecy is not the wish to see others judged.

words.note: Motah, the bar of a yoke, the wooden crosspiece laid on the animal's neck. Chapter 27 spoke of the whole yoke (ol) and its straps; here the word names the physical bar that Hananiah could snap. God's answer replaces it with bars of iron (verse 13).

Shavar, to break or shatter. Hananiah uses it of God breaking Babylon's yoke (verses 2, 4, 11) and of his own act (verses 10, 12). The same verb is used elsewhere for God breaking an oppressor's yoke in genuine deliverance (Leviticus 26:13), which is what makes Hananiah's words sound so plausible.
Barzel, iron. A yoke of iron cannot be broken by hand. Deuteronomy 28:48 threatens a yoke of iron as a covenant curse on a disobedient Israel, and verse 14 applies that curse to the present.

christ: The New Testament's warnings about false prophets carry the same concern as this chapter. Jesus warned that false prophets would come in sheep's clothing and that they would be known by their fruit (Matthew 7:15-20), and that many false prophets would arise and lead many astray (Matthew 24:11). His own ministry reversed Hananiah's pattern: he did not promise his followers quick political freedom but told them to take up their cross, and he announced the destruction of the temple rather than its immediate glory. Yet what Hananiah promised falsely, a broken yoke and a restored people, is what the prophets said God would truly do in his own time (Isaiah 9:4; Jeremiah 30:8), and the New Testament proclaims that Christ brings that deeper freedom, so that Paul can urge believers to stand firm and not submit again to a yoke of slavery (Galatians 5:1). The link here is thematic rather than a direct fulfillment of this chapter.

hard.q: Hananiah may have sincerely believed what he said. Why was his death a fair judgment?
hard.a: The chapter doesn't tell us Hananiah's motives, and he may well have believed he was speaking for God. His message drew on real promises: Isaiah had spoken of God breaking the oppressor's yoke, and in Hezekiah's day God had saved Jerusalem. But the Bible treats speaking in God's name as a sober responsibility with real consequences for others: Hananiah made the people trust in a lie (verse 15), which encouraged the rebellion that brought Jerusalem's destruction. The law of Deuteronomy 13 and 18 set the death penalty for a prophet who presumed to speak what God had not commanded, and here God carries out that sentence himself, not a mob. Readers who find this severe should notice that Jeremiah does not gloat. He hoped to be wrong (verse 6), withdrew from the confrontation (verse 11), and spoke the judgment only when God sent him back.

questions: Jeremiah answered Hananiah with “Amen” before he disagreed with him. How can you disagree with someone without wishing them to be wrong about good things?
Hananiah offered two years; Jeremiah said seventy. Why is a false short hope more dangerous than a true long one?
Jeremiah walked away and waited for God to speak before answering. When is silence the right response to a public challenge?
